newsitem.title: CHINA: China children opt to sue HK govt on deportation law.
newsitem.headline: China children opt to sue HK govt on deportation law.

text.p: Chinese children prepared on Thursday to sue the Hong Kong government over a law that will have illegal child immigrants deported to China.
A group of mainland-born children applied for legal aid to mount a court challenge to the legality of their deportation.
"I won't let them go. They are my flesh and blood," Choi, a mother of two China-born illegal immigrant children, said, weeping. "They are still so young."
Authorities said more than 30 children had so far sought legal aid and would hear by the weekend if their applications were successful, government radio reported.
The Legal Aid Department expected more applications to follow and was setting up a special team to handle the cases.
Local television reported more than 500 families were planning to fight the deportation order.

On Wednesday the new legislature installed after Britain handed Hong Kong back to China last week rubber-stamped a government bill allowing illegal child immigrants to be repatriated even if they have the right of abode here.
The smuggled children typically have at least one parent legally resident in Hong Kong and therefore have a theoretical right of abode under the territory's post-handover constitution, the Basic Law.

Hundreds, possibly thousands, of children have been smuggled into Hong Kong over the past year or so to join parents who already have residency rights. The alternative to sneaking in was a long wait for official migration clearance in China.

Tam Yiu-chung, a member of the cabinet of the territory's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, said the growing numbers of legal challenges against the new law came as no surprise, adding the court cases were inevitable.
"I think we cannot prohibit such kind of challenge," he said. "But of course we need to wait and see what is the court case, what is the High Court judges'...decision."
The heartbreak deportation law is under attack for violating the constitution and human rights.
Law professor Nihal Jayawickrama said the bill violated the Basic Law, which gives children the legal right to join parents who already are permanent residents.
"What's happening here is that the fundamental law of Hong Kong, the Basic Law, is being infringed upon right from the beginning," Jayawickrama said.

"Such an abrogation of these children's rights is particularly serious because it sets a precedent...of denying by administrative measures the constitutional rights of the Hong Kong people," the watchdog Hong Kong Human Rights Monitor said.
Martin Lee, chairman of the popular Democratic Party who was one of the former legislators ousted by Beijing upon Hong Kong's handover, also condemned the passage of the legislation.

"When it comes to the rule of law, no matter how many people are behind the government, the government must act within the law. And the most important law now that we have is our constitution, the Basic Law," he said.

Social worker Ho Hei-wah, who was helping the children seek legal aid, said he was stunned by the new rule. "I could never imagine that Tung Chee-hwa's government could destroy the entire system of the rule of law within just two weeks," he said.

But Tam said the bill did not contradict the Basic Law. "If the National People's Congress (China's parliament) finds that there is contradiction with the Basic Law, they will inform us. But we believe there is no contradiction," he said.

An estimated 66,000 mainland children are waiting to join parents in Hong Kong. The government hopes the new law will deter them from sneaking across in large numbers, and encourage them instead to go through proper formalities.
